<RichText>
# Vendoring vs. package-registry dependencies in a monorepo

**Run stats:** 2 participants, 2 extraction reports, 2 cross-reviews, 1 curator; started 2026-08-29T21:07:20Z. **Participants:** hermes · openai · gpt-5.6-luna · effort low; hermes · google · gemini-3.7-flash · effort low. **Curator:** hermes · openai · gpt-5.6-luna · effort low.
</RichText>

<Callout tone="warning">
This is multi-model synthesis, not verified truth. Both extractions draw on blog posts, documentation, and one arXiv paper — not peer-reviewed studies. Verify consequential claims before acting.
</Callout>

<Section title="Question">
<RichText>
When is it worth vendoring a third-party library into a monorepo instead of depending on the package registry, and what maintenance traps follow?
</RichText>
</Section>

<Section title="Final answer">
<RichText>
Vendoring a third-party library into a monorepo is worth it when the package registry cannot give you a guarantee you actually need, and you are willing to do the registry's job yourself. For the common case — a healthy, actively maintained library on a registry with lockfile and integrity-hash support (npm, Cargo, Go modules) — vendoring is almost never worth it; a lockfile with content hashes gives you reproducibility and integrity without the git-history and tooling costs (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**When to vendor:**

1. **Hermetic or offline-reproducible builds.** Air-gapped systems, regulated environments that must demonstrate rebuildability (medical FDA premarket, automotive UNECE R155), or build systems that structurally require local inputs (Bazel, Buck2, Pants). The sge-monorepo checks in all third-party code as policy, though Bazel's `http_archive` with a pinned `sha256` can also be hermetic without checked-in source — so hermeticity is one reason to vendor, not the only mechanism (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

2. **The upstream is abandoned, unmaintained, or you need a fork.** The registry serves a stale, buggy, or end-of-life version. Vendoring or a `replace`/`[patch]` directive lets you carry your fix. Distinguish two cases: an unmaintained library you vendor is a permanent adoption of its final state (no upstream patches ever); a live library you pin to an old version is temporary deferral that creates technical debt the moment you vendor it (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

3. **The registry is a supply-chain risk you cannot tolerate.** `left-pad` (2016) showed a trivial transitive dependency can vanish. For regulated or high-assurance environments, vendoring reintroduces a human checkpoint: nothing flows in without a person choosing it. The industry response was registry governance reform (unpublish policies) and local mirror caches (Artifactory), not blanket vendoring — but if your threat model requires import-time code review of the actual diff (including `postinstall` scripts), a lockfile alone cannot give you that (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

4. **Your ecosystem has no dominant registry or lockfile.** C/C++ never developed a universal package manager; SQLite and `stb` libraries are designed to be vendored as single amalgamation files (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

5. **You need to patch the dependency's source as part of your build** — platform-specific fixes, feature stripping, or static linking in ways a lockfile-only flow cannot express (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

**When not to vendor:** the ecosystem has good lockfile integrity hashes and frequent security releases (npm); the dependency graph is deep or fast-moving (vendoring one library often requires vendoring its entire transitive closure); or you have no update pipeline — vendoring without a scheduled re-vendor job is how you end up shipping 2019 (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**Maintenance traps that follow:**

- **Scanner invisibility.** SCA tools (Dependabot, npm audit, GitHub dependency graph) parse manifests and lockfiles; code copied into `vendor/` or `third_party/` with no manifest entry is outside enumeration. Some tools also exclude `vendor/` by default as noise. A dashboard reading "no known vulnerabilities" may be a false negative, not a true clean (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **Silent staleness.** Vendored code decays because no `npm audit` ever mentions it. The arXiv paper (2607.02059) found copied sources have a median age of 155 days, 38.5% are over one year old, only 4.3% document a recoverable origin, and 2.0% carry a checkable version (google · gemini-3.7-flash). A single-source audit blog reported a median age of over three years for vendored C libraries; the exact number is anecdotal, but the directional claim — vendored code rots quietly — is confirmed by every source (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **License compliance.** Vendoring a library means copying its LICENSE file into your tree and becoming a distributor. Attribution requirements (Apache/MIT), copyleft contamination risk (GPL/AGPL), and dual-license disambiguation all fall on you. A registry dependency keeps license metadata in the manifest; a vendored copy loses it. In a monorepo with many consumers, a single vendored GPL library creates compliance questions for every downstream package (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **In-place edits create a silent fork with no CVE identifier.** The moment someone edits vendored code directly, it diverges from any upstream version a CVE database tracks, and upstream patches no longer apply cleanly. Local changes must live as separate patch files applied at build time (pnpm patch, patch-package, quilt-style dirs) so the vendored tree stays byte-identical to a known upstream commit (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **Git history cost.** Git clones the entire repository history by default; a vendored dependency updated 20 times means 20 snapshots in `.git` forever. Vendoring was cheap under SVN (you never downloaded old revisions) and expensive under Git — a cost teams inheriting SVN-era conventions may not realize they are paying (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

- **`go mod vendor` silently destroys local patches.** If someone edits a vendored Go dependency and another developer runs `go mod vendor`, the edits are replaced with the upstream version with no warning. The correct fork mechanism is a `replace` directive, not editing `vendor/` (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

- **Transitive closure explosion.** Vendoring a single library often requires vendoring everything it depends on. Package managers exist to manage exactly this closure automatically; replacing that automation with explicit ownership is sometimes desirable and sometimes overwhelming (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **Split-brain.** Vendoring a library in one part of a monorepo while depending on the registry version elsewhere produces two copies at potentially different versions with no consistency mechanism. Package A might vendor `foo@1.2` while package B depends on `foo@1.3` from the registry — same import name, different code (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

- **Build-time tool coupling.** A vendored gRPC library may require a specific `protoc` plugin version; vendoring the library without vendoring the plugin creates a hidden coupling to the registry for the build tool, defeating the offline-reproducibility goal while appearing to satisfy it (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

- **Re-vendor diff conflicts.** A large vendored refresh produces a diff that conflicts with concurrent feature branches in a monorepo, forcing thousands of vendored-file lines to be resolved during rebase even when there is no semantic conflict (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

- **SBOM incompleteness.** SBOM generators that derive from manifests and lockfiles (CycloneDX, Syft in lockfile mode, `cargo cyclonedx`) omit vendored code entirely, producing an incomplete SBOM. A regulated environment accepting that SBOM will have silent gaps for every vendored dependency (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

- **Code review fatigue.** A 50,000-line vendoring PR generates "LGTM" fatigue; the argument that "you can read your dependencies" is weakened by the reality that big dumps get careless reviews (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).

**Best practices that keep vendoring safe:** keep the manifest (so scanners still know exact versions); use one declared vendor directory with an `UPSTREAM` file per component; never edit in place — keep patches in `patches/` applied at build; automate re-vendoring on a schedule; scan the tree, not just the manifest. Go's `go mod vendor` is the best-behaved form because `vendor/modules.txt` preserves version identity, though it does not record content hashes (those live in `go.sum`) — Cargo's `cargo vendor` is arguably stronger because `Cargo.lock` records hashes and is used alongside the vendored tree (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

<Section title="Knowledge map">
<Tabs>
<Tab label="Shared core">
<RichText>
Claims both extractions made independently — repetition, not proof:

- Vendoring trades registry-time risk for repo-time risk: builds become immutable and immune to upstream deletion, at the cost of hiding the dependency from scanners and freezing vulnerabilities (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- SCA scanners (Dependabot, npm audit, GitHub dependency graph) lose visibility into vendored code — manifest-based enumeration misses code copied into vendor/ or third_party/ (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Lockfiles with content hashes provide reproducibility and integrity without vendoring for most ecosystems, making vendoring unnecessary when the registry and lockfile are healthy (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Vendoring a single library often requires vendoring its entire transitive closure; package managers exist to manage this automatically (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Best practices converge: keep the manifest, one vendor directory, no in-place edits (patches/ applied at build), automated re-vendoring on a schedule, scan the tree not just the manifest (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- The honest default for most teams in fast-moving ecosystems with good lockfile integrity is: do not vendor (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
- Go's `go mod vendor` preserves manifest metadata (vendor/modules.txt), making it the best-behaved vendoring form; Cargo's `cargo vendor` preserves Cargo.lock hashes alongside the vendored tree (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).
</RichText>
</Tab>

<RichText>
Kept even with a support count of one — consensus is repetition, not truth:

- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** The SVN-vs-Git cost asymmetry — vendoring was cheap under SVN (current revision only) and expensive under Git (full history, every snapshot forever).
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** `go mod vendor` silently destroys local patches; the `replace` directive is the correct fork mechanism.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Vendoring can make code review worse — 50,000-line dumps get careless "LGTM" reviews.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** File-level copying is an invisible "Type-II supply chain" — the arXiv paper found copying more often signals "upstream bypass" than "offline availability."
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Nix/Guix are the philosophical endpoint of the vendoring instinct — they vendor the entire build closure into a content-addressed store without the git-history cost.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Registries can serve different bytes for the same version without content hashes — a version pin alone is insufficient; integrity hashes are the real replacement for vendoring.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** EOL dependencies are a compliance problem, not just security — under HIPAA, HITRUST, or PCI, carrying a dependency that will never receive updates may be non-compliant; vendoring makes it worse by hiding it from scanners.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** Enterprise proxy caches (Artifactory) close the availability gap without vendoring; the industry response to left-pad was registry governance reform, not blanket vendoring.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only:** The "Against Convenience" essay frames vendoring as a security firebreak — every package becomes a firebreak because nothing updates without a human choosing to.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Some SCA scanners exclude `vendor/` by default as noise — vendoring makes a dependency invisible in two compounding ways: no manifest entry and an explicit ignore rule.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Tamper-resistance is not a differentiator between vendoring and a lockfile; vendoring uniquely buys availability (survives registry deletion/outage) and import-time code review of the actual diff.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** A vendored malicious package is worse for initial import but better afterward — it cannot self-update, and code review and code-scanning can catch it, but no registry-side takedown will save you automatically.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** SBOM provenance degrades for hand-copied code — NTIA minimum elements require supplier and version per component; "some files we copied in 2021" satisfies neither.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** The "healthy friction" argument cuts both ways — friction is good at intake (selectivity) and bad at maintenance (staleness); the deciding factor is whether you couple it with an automated re-vendor pipeline.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Repo size/diff dominance — large vendored refreshes obscure meaningful changes to the project's own code, making review and merging harder in a monorepo.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Monorepo-specific "copy into each app" cost — unless the source repository supports reusable source modules, you may need multiple copies of the same vendored dependency across apps.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only:** Git submodules/subtrees are "vendoring with an audit trail" — the pointer to upstream survives, mitigating provenance and update traps.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only (via cross-review):** Quantified staleness from arXiv — copied sources have a median age of 155 days, 38.5% over one year, 4.3% document origin, 2.0% carry a checkable version.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only (via cross-review):** License-risk visibility loss — the arXiv paper found 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only (via cross-review):** License compliance as a first-order maintenance trap — attribution, copyleft contamination, dual-license disambiguation.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only (via cross-review):** Build-system-native vendoring (Bazel, Buck2, Pants) as a structural requirement, not a tradeoff choice.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only (via cross-review):** Split-brain trap — vendoring in one part of a monorepo while depending on the registry version elsewhere.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only (via cross-review):** Build-time tool dependencies (protoc plugins, code generators) must also be vendored when you vendor their runtime consumers.
- **gpt-5.6-luna only (via cross-review):** Re-vendor diff conflicts in monorepos with automated merges — spurious conflicts that consume engineering time even with no semantic conflict.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only (via cross-review):** SBOM/compliance dimension — CycloneDX, Syft in lockfile mode, and cargo cyclonedx omit vendored code, producing an incomplete SBOM.
- **gemini-3.7-flash only (via cross-review):** `git subtree`/submodule as a middle-ground mechanism that keeps upstream-tracking history in-tree while avoiding the registry.

<Tab label="Contradictions">
<RichText>
**1. "Vendoring improves security" vs. "vendoring degrades security visibility" (unresolved, threat-model-dependent).**

Vendoring prevents automatic propagation of malicious updates — a supply-chain integrity benefit. But vendored code is invisible to SCA scanners — a supply-chain visibility cost. Both are true under different threat models; the net effect depends on which threat matters more to your organization. Neither report resolves this; both present both sides (openai · gpt-5.6-luna; google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**2. Bazel hermeticity requires vendoring vs. Bazel can be hermetic without checked-in code (challenged by cross-review).**

openai · gpt-5.6-luna frames hermeticity and vendoring as tightly coupled: "Vendoring is how you get hermeticity, so all third-party code lives in the repository." google · gemini-3.7-flash challenges this: Bazel's `http_archive` with a pinned `sha256` downloads the dependency at build time and verifies it, making the build hermetic without checked-in source. The sge-monorepo chose to check everything in as policy, not toolchain constraint. The claim should be qualified from "the way" to "one way" (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**3. "Healthy friction makes you selective" vs. "friction compounds into staleness" (resolved by reconciliation).**

dfetch argues requiring a conscious pull-in makes teams more selective about dependencies. Safeguard argues the same friction compounds into staleness. These are not contradictory — they describe the same force at different timescales. Friction is good at intake and bad at maintenance; the deciding factor is whether you couple it with an automated re-vendor pipeline (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**4. Meta/Buck2 "vendor all third-party code" — under-sourced (unresolved).**

openai · gpt-5.6-luna lists Meta alongside Google as a monorepo that "vendor[s] all third-party code," but the cited Nesbitt article discusses only Google's monorepo in detail. Buck2 documentation describes third-party dependencies imported as Git submodules or generated via `reindeer` from Crates.io — external fetch mechanisms, not blanket check-in. The claim is plausible for Meta's internal practice but needs a Meta-specific citation (google · gemini-3.7-flash).

**5. "Lockfile pins content as hard as committed bytes" vs. "you need to review postinstall scripts" (intra-report tension).**

google · gemini-3.7-flash claims a lockfile's `sha512` integrity fields pin content "just as hard as committed bytes" (Claim 2) and also lists postinstall script review as a reason to vendor (condition 5). A lockfile pins content but does not protect against malicious code executing at install time — the hash confirms the bytes are what you expect, but those bytes include the script. Vendoring enables pre-execution review; a lockfile does not. These are different properties, not equivalent ones (openai · gpt-5.6-luna).
</RichText>
